title: What AI Benchmarks Actually Measure: Adapting Convergent and Discriminant Validity to Interrogate Fifty-Six AI Benchmarks
note: arXiv:2609.08812v1, submitted 8 September 2026, CC BY 4.0. This report's central source — the 9 hypothesis-test statistics, ΔAUC values, and citations to Tables A.2/C.1/E.1 are all drawn from this version.

title: madesai/what-ai-benchmarks-actually-measure (dataset)
note: CC BY 4.0. Per-model scores and item identifiers only — item text itself is not released; the data card states it does not distribute benchmark prompts.

title: BBQ: A Hand-Built Bias Benchmark for Question Answering
container-title: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2022
note: Introduces a separate bias score because accuracy alone cannot capture response patterns among wrong answers (§5 Evaluation); §9 Ethical Considerations warns not to read a low bias score as evidence of an unbiased model.

title: Convergent and discriminant validation by the multitrait-multimethod matrix
note: The source from which reference 1 draws its three considerations of convergence, discrimination, and method effects. Full text not accessible (APA paywall) — cited here only via reference 1's own summary.

title: Revealing the structure of language model capabilities
note: This is 2023a — the factor-analysis paper reference 1 §2 correctly cites for the claim that BBQ accuracy loads more strongly on a reasoning factor than a bias factor. That analysis has no bias factor; loadings are shown only as heatmap color (Figure 1), not numbers, and it makes no reclassification recommendation. §4.4 of reference 1 misattributes the same result to the authors' different 2023b (Science) paper.

title: Safetywashing: Do AI Safety Benchmarks Actually Measure Safety Progress?
container-title: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37, pp. 68559-68594
note: Prior large-scale audit of safety-benchmark/capability correlation. On bias specifically, its conclusion runs the opposite direction of reference 1 (Table 4: bias benchmarks not strongly correlated with capability/compute for chat models), while separately reporting BBQ's disambiguated split correlates with capability at 76.8%.

title: Stereotyping Norwegian Salmon: An Inventory of Pitfalls in Fairness Benchmark Datasets
note: Warns that the same pitfalls can arise wherever contrastive pairs are constructed to measure computationally-defined harms — cited by reference 1 in a footnote. The reason not to read this report's §5 prescription (contrastive-pair design) on its own.

title: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM)
note: The source reference 1 collected benchmarks from, and the comparison standard for its format-compliance screen. HELM covers 51 benchmarks and 142 models — reference 1 has more benchmarks, HELM has more models.

title: KoBBQ: Korean Bias Benchmark for Question Answering
container-title: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics
note: 268 templates, 76,048 samples, 12 categories — do not conflate with the July 2023 preprint's 246 templates and 4,740 samples. Inherits BBQ's two-score structure but changes the diff-bias score's denominator and rescaling.

title: HyperCLOVA X Technical Report
note: A case of a Korean lab voluntarily reporting BBQ and KoBBQ on both accuracy and diff-bias axes. §6.4's denominator is this report's own test-split sample, not the full size of KoBBQ.

title: System cards, model cards, technical reports and launch announcements for 11 commercial model releases
note: OpenAI GPT-5, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4; Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.6; Google DeepMind Gemini 3 Pro, Gemini 3.1 Pro; xAI Grok 4.1, Grok 4.20 Beta; DeepSeek V3.1; Alibaba Qwen3. Checked September 2026 — the right-hand column of the section 6.1 comparison table.

title: Four frontier AI risk frameworks
note: Anthropic Responsible Scaling Policy v2.2; OpenAI Preparedness Framework v2 (15 April 2025); Google Frontier Safety Framework v3.1 (17 April 2026); xAI Risk Management Framework (20 August 2025). Section 6.3's check is confined to these specific versions.

title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile (NIST AI 600-1)

author.literal: National Institute of Standards and Technology

note: Section 7.1's verbatim quote is the full text of item MS-2.11-001, confirmed directly against the official PDF. NIST AI RMF 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1, https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.100-1.pdf), cited alongside it, requires the concept only, with no benchmark named.

title: EU AI Act, Korea's AI Framework Act, and the TTA AI trustworthiness certification checklist
note: EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) Article 55(1)(a) and Annex XI, plus the GPAI Code of Practice (10 July 2025); Korea's AI Framework Act and Article 28 of its enforcement decree; the TTA AI trustworthiness certification checklist. Grounds for the judgments in sections 6.3 and 6.4 — a search of all four frontier risk frameworks turns up zero uses of "fairness" or "discrimination."

title: schema_classic.yaml

title: EvalEval Coalition
note: An evaluation-infrastructure consortium hosted by Hugging Face, the University of Edinburgh, and EleutherAI; released an Evaluation Cards beta on 9 June 2026. The concrete form of the shared infrastructure that §5 of reference 1 points to.

title: Taxonomy and Consistency Analysis of Safety Benchmarks for AI Agents
note: Classifies LLM-as-judge as "the dominant paradigm" for safety-benchmark scoring. Paired in section 4.3 with Zhang, Xinran, "How Sensitive Are Safety Benchmarks to Judge Configuration Choices?" (arXiv:2604.24074), which reports result consistency dropping from 100% to 43.5% depending on judge configuration. No single aggregate figure for the share of safety benchmarks scored by an LLM judge exists across the field.
